hub_subtitle: From hesitant communicator to confident global business leader

lesson.menu_desc: Milton can no longer be the only person who sells the brand in English. Today he interviews Rachel, a candidate for export sales manager in the US office, and learns the questions that really test a person: hypothetical ones (suppose a client asked for a discount, what would you do? what would you have done if...?). Plus the language of hiring and leading: candidate, shortlist, recruit, track record, delegate, accountable, turnover, mentor — 35 slides

listenings.text: Hi Milton, this is Megan from the recruitment agency. Quick update on the export sales manager job. We received sixty applications, and we've put five candidates on the shortlist. Two of them have a strong track record in luxury jewelry, which is rare. My advice for the interviews is simple. Don't only ask people what they did. Ask them what they would do. Suppose a client complained about a late delivery. What would they say? Imagine they had to recruit their own team. Where would they start? The answers tell you much more than an application. One more thing. Turnover in this kind of job is high in New York, around thirty percent a year, so talk about salary early. If we lost a great candidate at the end because of money, it would be a waste for everyone. I'll send you the five profiles tonight.

The worst hire of my career taught me the best lesson. Ten years ago, I recruited a brilliant salesman. Great track record, great energy, great smile. But I never asked him a single hypothetical question. If I had asked him what he would do when a client got angry, I would have seen the problem in five minutes. He didn't like to listen. In the first six months, we lost three good clients. Today I do two things differently. First, I ask every candidate the same question: suppose you made a big mistake with a client, what would you do the next morning? The good ones talk about responsibility. They're accountable. Second, I learned to delegate. A leader who does everything alone builds a team that can't do anything alone. If you want your people to grow, give them real responsibility, and be a mentor, not just a boss.
